backgroundImageAltText: Four-panel illustration of skin appendages: hair follicle with arrector pili, sebaceous gland opening into a follicle, eccrine sweat gland with coiled base and straight duct, and a longitudinal section of a fingernail.

params.text: Hair grows from the follicle base (hair bulb), which caps a vascular dermal papilla. The arrector pili muscle, supplied by sympathetic nerves, contracts to raise the hair (goose flesh). Hair is absent from palms, soles, the red margin of the lips and the glans penis. The follicle lining is living epidermis — its cells can regenerate the surface after a partial-thickness burn.

Sebaceous glands open into hair follicles and secrete sebum by holocrine secretion (the whole cell breaks down to release its product). They are absent from the palms and soles. Blockage of a duct causes acne or a sebaceous cyst. Like the follicle, the gland epithelium can resurface a wound from within.

Eccrine glands are found all over the body and are densest on the palms, soles and forehead. They secrete a watery sweat for thermoregulation (merocrine secretion). Apocrine glands, found in the axilla and groin, open into hair follicles and produce a thicker secretion whose bacterial breakdown causes body odour.

The nail is a plate of hard keratin — a modified stratum corneum. It grows continuously from the nail matrix (root) under the proximal nail fold. The lunula is the pale crescent visible through the nail plate. Nails protect the fingertips and improve fine touch by providing counter-pressure on the pulp.
